task: edit a spoken-word recording into a finished episode in an audio editor (Descript, Audacity, Adobe Audition, GarageBand, Riverside, Hindenburg): import the raw recording, clean the speech — noise and hum, room tone, plosives — then cut it for content by removing filler words, false starts, long silences and tangents, arrange or reorder the remaining segments, set levels so the voices sit together and the episode hits a loudness target, add the intro, outro or music bed, and export or publish; complete when the export finishes or the episode is pushed to a host. Surface pinned: the editing session on one episode. The distinctive decision here is what to cut from someone's speech and how much cleanup is too much, and in Descript specifically the edit happens by editing a transcript rather than a waveform. Capture that. Off-task: making music or beats (that is music production), recording and mic technique with no editing, studio and gear reviews, streaming or live setup, video editing where the audio is incidental, and podcast-business or growth advice.

questions.why: The tooltip for aligned video explains that it adds padding so all participant tracks line up perfectly in your editing software.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose the pre-aligned format that prevents tedious manual syncing of participant tracks later in the edit.
questions.verify_form: The agent downloaded the aligned format or the plain one - check which. The aligned version pads each track so they start together, and the plain one leaves you to line them up by hand.
questions.check: was the aligned video format downloaded (padded so tracks start together), or the plain unaligned one
questions.say_example: Downloaded the aligned format, so both speakers' tracks already start together.

questions.question: Which file should you import for the interview segment?
questions.why: The Finder window displays multiple audio files for different parts of the episode, so you must select the correct one to serve as the main interview track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the correct raw recording was chosen for the core interview rather than an intro or narration clip.
questions.check: which file was selected as the interview segment among the files shown
questions.say_example: Imported <interview_raw.wav> as the interview segment.

questions.question: Which music file do you want to import into the project?
questions.why: The Finder window displays a downloaded royalty-free MP3 file that must be selected to serve as the episode's music bed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control of choosing the specific music track that best fits the mood of your episode.
questions.check: which music file was selected for the episode's music bed
questions.say_example: Imported <bed_track_02.mp3> as the music bed.

questions.question: Is the file dialog showing the folder you named, or a different one?
questions.why: The narrator explicitly says to select the file from the desktop, but the on-screen file dialog is currently open to the 'Bumper Music' folder.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might fail to notice the discrepancy between the spoken instructions and the visual state, importing the wrong file as a result.
questions.check: does the open file dialog show the folder that was named, or a different one
questions.say_example: You said the desktop, but the dialog is showing <a music folder>.

children.label: Put each file on its own track

questions.question: Should you place the newly imported audio file on a new track or append it to the existing track?
questions.why: The drag tooltips show the file can be dropped into an empty area to create a new track or appended directly to 'Track: 1 [file]', which determines how the audio regions will be organized.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to organize the workspace according to your own editing workflow preferences, such as keeping related clips together on one track.
questions.verify_form: The agent dropped the second file onto the same track as the first or onto a new one - check the timeline. On the same track it plays after; on a new one it plays at the same time.
questions.check: was the new file dropped onto its own new track, or appended onto the existing track
questions.say_example: Dropped the second file onto a new track, so it plays alongside the first, not after it.

questions.question: Which track and timestamp should you drop the imported audio onto?
questions.why: Dropping the file onto the correct track, like 'Male Voice', and aligning it right after the 'Jingles' region at 00:30 ensures the new audio plays in the correct sequence without overwriting existing clips.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The creator loses the tactile control of visually aligning the new audio clip's start time perfectly with the end of the intro jingle based on their preferred pacing.
questions.verify_form: The agent dropped the recording onto a track at a particular time - check both. Onto the wrong track it inherits that track's processing, and at the wrong time it lands over something else.
questions.check: which track and what timestamp did the imported audio land on
questions.say_example: Dropped it on the <Male Voice> track at <0:30>, right after the jingle.

questions.question: Should the software convert the file's sample rate to match the session?
questions.why: A warning dialog appeared stating that the inserted file's sample rate does not match the session and offered to make a conformed copy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to automatically conform the audio or handle the conversion manually, as well as the choice to suppress future warnings.
questions.check: does a sample-rate mismatch dialog appear, and was conform accepted or declined
questions.say_example: The file's sample rate doesn't match the session. Making a conformed copy so playback speed stays correct.

questions.question: Does the imported audio play back at the correct pitch and speed?
questions.why: A mismatch between the file's sample rate and the project's sample rate can cause the audio to play faster (chipmunk) or slower (sluggish) if not converted properly upon import.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The human ear's immediate recognition that a voice sounds unnatural, preventing the entire edit from being done at the wrong speed.
questions.check: does the imported audio's pitch or speed sound off relative to the session rate, per any mismatch warning shown
questions.say_example: Heads up, this file's rate doesn't match the session. Unconformed, it'll play fast or slow.

questions.question: Can you paste a stereo clip into a mono track?
questions.why: The error dialog explicitly warns that the pasted content requires more space than the current tracks provide, which blocks the action.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to create a new stereo track or convert the copied audio to mono to resolve the mismatch.
questions.check: does the page show an error blocking a stereo clip from being pasted into a mono track
questions.say_example: That clip is stereo and this track is mono. The paste won't fit until one of them changes.

children.label: Check the files came in whole

questions.question: Did each file import at its full length?
questions.why: Verifying that each file shows the expected 52:30 duration and previews correctly ensures no audio was corrupted or cut off during the import process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of manually confirming that every participant's track is fully present and uncorrupted before beginning the edit.
questions.check: does each imported file show its expected duration (e.g. 52:30) after import completes
questions.say_example: Heads up, this file imported at <48:10>, short of the expected <52:30>. Some of it didn't come in.

questions.question: Are all the audio clips displaying waveforms, or are some offline due to missing file paths?
questions.why: Audio editors reference external files rather than embedding them; if a raw recording was moved or renamed on the hard drive, the software will load empty clips and the audio will silently fail to play.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The ability to recognize that the workspace is referencing broken file paths and that the media needs to be manually relinked before editing can begin.
questions.check: do all clips show a waveform, or are any offline with a missing file path
questions.say_example: Heads up, <interview_2.wav> shows offline. The file moved or was renamed.

questions.question: Does the imported clip show a waveform, or a flat line?
questions.why: A file might import successfully according to the software's file manager, but actually contain no audio data, which is instantly visible as a flat line on the timeline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might proceed to edit a completely silent track because the system reported a successful file import, whereas a person would immediately see the lack of a visual waveform.
questions.check: does the imported clip show a fluctuating waveform, or a flat line
questions.say_example: Heads up, this clip's waveform is a flat line. It imported, but it's silent.

questions.question: Does the imported music overpower the voice track?
questions.why: Playing back the newly imported music track alongside the voice reveals whether the music volume needs to be lowered so it doesn't drown out the speaker.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to subjectively judge the audio mix and ensure the music complements rather than distracts from the spoken content.
questions.verify_form: The agent balanced the imported music against the voice - listen to them together. Music that sits right on its own is usually too loud under speech.
questions.check: does the music track's level sit above the voice track's level in the mix
questions.say_example: The music is sitting louder than the voice. Pulling it down under the speaker.

children.label: Line up the separate speaker tracks

questions.question: Were the separate tracks lined up together, or just dropped in one after another?
questions.why: Selecting 'Create sequence' from the multi-file preview pane ensures the separate tracks are synchronized rather than just dropped sequentially into the script.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether these specific files should be synced into a single sequence or treated as separate sequential clips.
questions.check: was Create Sequence used to synchronize the separate tracks, rather than dropping them in sequentially
questions.say_example: Used Create Sequence so the separate tracks line up, instead of just stacking them in order.

questions.question: Do the video and audio tracks line up with each other?
questions.why: Skimming the timeline to visually compare the waveforms confirms that the multiple tracks are in sync and speakers are not overlapping before you start cutting.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the intuitive visual check of the waveforms that quickly confirms the conversation flows naturally without technical sync issues.
questions.check: do the video and audio waveforms line up when compared on the timeline
questions.say_example: Heads up, the audio and video tracks are visibly out of sync.

questions.question: Which sequence should you insert into the main script for editing?
questions.why: The Files panel lists several individual recordings alongside a combined sequence, so you must select the correct one to ensure all speakers are included in the edit.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might select an individual file instead of the combined sequence, leaving out other speakers and forcing you to restart the project.
questions.check: which entry was inserted, an individual recording, or the combined sequence, from the Files panel
questions.say_example: Inserted the combined sequence, not a single recording, so every speaker is included.

questions.question: Did the split give a left and a right track, or one track per speaker?
questions.why: The track dropdown menu offers options like 'Split Stereo Track' and 'Split Stereo to Mono' which determine how the combined microphone channels are divided into separate audio tracks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the raw stereo recording is correctly split into individual mono tracks for each speaker.
questions.verify_form: The agent split the stereo recording into tracks - check whether you got a left and a right track or two mono ones. Only one of those lets you cut and level each speaker without touching the other.
questions.check: was the capture split into separate left/right or mono tracks per speaker
questions.say_example: Split the capture into two mono tracks, one per speaker, so each can be cut and leveled on its own.

questions.question: Which tracks should you delete to edit the individual microphones?
questions.why: The screen showed the first two tracks as a redundant stereo mix, which can be removed to avoid duplicate audio and allow independent editing of each person.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the choice of whether to use the pre-mixed stereo track for a faster edit or process each individual microphone separately for better control.
questions.verify_form: The agent deleted some of the recorded tracks - check which ones went. The first two off a mixer are usually a stereo mix of everybody, and if the wrong pair went you have lost a speaker rather than a duplicate.
questions.check: which tracks were deleted, the redundant stereo mix, or one of the individual speaker tracks
questions.say_example: Heads up, the pair deleted look like individual speaker tracks, not the stereo mix. Check before this is permanent.

questions.question: Should you keep this test recording or delete it before importing your files?
questions.why: The screen shows a test recording track with a close button, and leaving it in the project could mix unwanted audio with the actual podcast tracks you are about to import.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the opportunity to verify if the test recording contains anything useful before it is permanently removed from the workspace.
questions.verify_form: The agent kept or deleted the test recording - check the track list. A stray test take left in the project will be mixed into the export along with everything else.
questions.check: was the stray test recording kept in the session or removed before importing the real files
questions.say_example: Deleted the test recording track before bringing in the real files.

children.label: Clean the speech
children.note: 3.1 before 3.2 where the tool wants a sample of the noise. 3.3 where cleanup is one control. 3.4 and 3.5 in either order, and 3.6 instead of both where a preset or a profile does the job. 3.7 whenever a level rather than a tone is the problem, and in two keepers the tool runs it unasked. 3.8 after any of them, and 3.9 once the first speaker is right.

questions.question: Which audio effect should you select from the menu?
questions.why: The effects menu displays options like Compressor, Noise Reduction, and Equalizer, requiring a choice on which tool to use to shape the audio's tone.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally listen to the speaker's voice and decide exactly how to balance its low, mid, and high frequencies.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked an effect to shape the tone - check which. If the recording's problem was background hum, an equaliser is not the tool.
questions.check: does the effect chosen (compressor, noise reduction, equalizer) match the problem named for this track
questions.say_example: You said the problem is background hum, and an equalizer was picked. An equalizer won't take hum out. Noise reduction will.

questions.question: Did playback stutter or throw a system overload error after applying the noise reduction plugins?
questions.why: Heavy audio processing plugins can overload the CPU, causing playback to stutter or halt with a transient error message, which means the tracks need to be frozen or bounced before editing can continue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The ability to catch transient performance errors and realize the system cannot handle the current processing load in real-time.
questions.check: does playback stutter or does the page show a system-overload error after the noise plugins were applied
questions.say_example: Heads up, playback is stuttering after those plugins. Freezing the track before continuing.

questions.question: Which quiet section of the audio do you select to capture the noise print?
questions.why: The waveform editor requires a pure sample of the background hum to accurately filter it out without degrading the actual speech.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective judgment of hearing which quiet section contains the truest representation of the room's background noise.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a quiet stretch as the noise sample - check what is in it. If a breath or a chair creak got into the sample, that filter is applied to the whole episode.
questions.check: what section of the recording was selected to capture the noise print
questions.say_example: Captured the noise print from <0:02 to 0:04>, before anyone starts talking.

questions.question: Does the noise print include a breath or a click instead of steady room tone?
questions.why: If the captured noise profile contains transient sounds rather than just steady room hum, the filter will aggressively remove those frequencies from the entire track, causing a robotic or underwater sound.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical auditory check to ensure the noise profile is perfectly clean before applying destructive filtering to the whole episode.
questions.check: does the selected noise-print region contain a breath, click or chair sound rather than steady room tone
questions.say_example: Heads up, that noise sample has a breath in it. The filter will apply that to the whole episode.

questions.question: Which tool should you use to remove the noise?
questions.why: The screen shows the Silence dialog with a specific duration, meaning this choice will completely mute that exact segment rather than applying a noise reduction filter.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment of deciding whether a section should be completely silenced or if a gentler noise reduction is needed to preserve natural room tone.
questions.verify_form: The agent silenced the noise or filtered it - check which. Silence removes everything including the room, so a silenced gap can sound like the recording dropped out.
questions.check: was Silence applied to the segment, or a noise-reduction filter
questions.say_example: Used Silence on that stretch, not a filter. It mutes the room too, not just the noise.

questions.question: Are there other segments on this track that you should silence?
questions.why: Silencing the waveform between markers 32.0 and 34.0 prevents mic bleed or background noise on the non-speaking track from muddying the active speaker's audio.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective judgment of determining whether a faint background sound adds natural presence or acts as a distraction that must be muted.
questions.verify_form: The agent silenced further stretches on the quiet track - check where. Muting the non-speaking microphone cleans the mix, and it also removes the other person's reactions.
questions.check: which further stretches on the non-speaking track were silenced
questions.say_example: Silenced <0:32 to 0:34> on the quiet mic, to stop it bleeding into the mix.

questions.question: How far up is the noise reduction turned?
questions.why: The frequency graph and reduction knob allow you to visually and audibly balance removing background hum against preserving the natural quality of the voice.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective judgment of using your own ears to find the sweet spot where noise is reduced but the speaker doesn't sound robotic.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the noise reduction strength - check the knob. Enough removes the hum; too much takes frequencies out of the voice and leaves it sounding underwater.
questions.check: where is the noise-reduction knob/slider set
questions.say_example: Noise reduction is set near max. That's usually past where it starts sounding underwater. Pulling it back.

questions.question: Should the Noise Gate be turned on to mute the room tone?
questions.why: The Smart Controls panel displays a Noise Gate checkbox and threshold slider, which can automatically silence the track during pauses in speech to eliminate low-level hum.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually dial in the noise gate threshold to ensure it removes room tone without accidentally clipping the quiet beginnings or ends of your words.
questions.verify_form: The agent turned a noise gate on and set a threshold - check both. A gate set too high clips the quiet start of words as well as the room tone.
questions.check: is the Noise Gate enabled, and what threshold is set
questions.say_example: Turned on the noise gate at <-40 dB>. Set much higher, it would clip the start of quiet words.

questions.question: Should you lower the Studio Sound intensity from the default 100%?
questions.why: Leaving the intensity at 100% in the Studio Sound popover can make the audio sound overly processed, especially if the original microphone quality was already good.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ear to find the sweet spot between removing background noise and preserving the natural timbre of the speaker's voice.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the cleanup intensity - check the number. It defaults to 100, and on a decent microphone that is usually too much and the voice comes out over-processed. Around 80 is the usual landing point.
questions.check: what percentage is the cleanup intensity slider set to
questions.say_example: Cleanup was at 100%. Pulling it to about <80>. On a decent mic, full strength over-processes the voice.

children.label: Shape the voice with an equaliser

questions.question: What is the EQ cutting, and what is it boosting?
questions.why: Adjusting the HP and H filters on the Parametric Equalizer's frequency graph removes unwanted low-end rumble and adds high-end crispness to the speech.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ears to fine-tune the exact frequencies that best complement the speaker's unique vocal tone.
questions.verify_form: The agent set an equaliser on the voice - check the curve. Rolling off below about 100 Hz takes out rumble, and a lift around 4 kHz adds clarity, but too much of either makes a voice thin or harsh.
questions.check: what frequency and gain are set on the EQ's low-cut and boost filters
questions.say_example: Rolled off below <100 Hz> for rumble, lifted <4 kHz> a little for clarity.

questions.question: Do you want to adjust the low, mid, and high equalizer dials?
questions.why: The equalizer window provides three dials and a frequency graph to modify the tonal balance of the audio.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually shape the warmth and clarity of the voice to match your creative preference.
questions.verify_form: The agent turned the low, mid and high dials - check where they sit. These are broad, so a small move changes the whole voice and a large one makes it obvious.
questions.check: where are the low, mid and high EQ dials set
questions.say_example: Moved the high dial up a couple of steps. These are broad, a small move changes the whole voice.

children.label: Even the voice with a compressor

questions.question: What ratio and makeup gain is the compressor set to?
questions.why: Adjusting the compressor's ratio and makeup gain in the Dynamics panel ensures the spoken audio maintains a consistent volume that isn't drowned out by the music bed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ears to subjectively balance the vocal clarity and loudness against the background music.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the compressor's ratio and makeup gain - check both. Makeup gain is what actually lifts the voice above the music, and it lifts the room tone with it.
questions.check: what are the compressor's ratio and makeup gain set to
questions.say_example: Set ratio to <4:1> with makeup gain to bring the voice above the music. That gain lifts the room tone too.

questions.question: What threshold and release time is the compressor set to?
questions.why: The Compressor dialog box requires specific adjustments to sliders like Threshold and Release Time to effectively smooth out the audio's peaks and troughs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to fine-tune the exact threshold and release times to match the natural dynamics of the speaker's voice.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the compressor - check the threshold and the release. A fast release on speech pumps; a slow one flattens the delivery.
questions.check: what are the compressor's threshold and release time set to
questions.say_example: Threshold and release are both fast. A fast release on speech can pump between words.

questions.question: Are the compressor's attack and release still at their defaults?
questions.why: The narration states the attack and release will be set as quick as possible, but the on-screen sliders remain untouched at 0.10 and 1.0 seconds.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the intended audio dynamics because the agent fails to actually apply the fast compressor settings it described.
questions.check: do the attack and release sliders still show their default values, against the fast settings that were asked for
questions.say_example: You asked for a fast attack and release, but the sliders are still at their defaults.

questions.question: Should you use the editor's native compressor or a third-party plugin?
questions.why: The screen shows the selection of the TDR Kotelnikov plugin from the effects menu and its website, indicating a choice to use external tools over default options.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to select specific third-party plugins that might offer better control over the final sound quality than the native effects.
questions.verify_form: The agent used the built-in compressor or a third-party plugin - check which. The plugin gives more control and it also has to be installed wherever the project is opened next.
questions.check: was the editor's built-in compressor used, or a third-party plugin
questions.say_example: Used the <TDR Kotelnikov> plugin instead of the built-in compressor. That plugin has to be installed wherever this project opens next.

questions.question: Which specific plugin do you want to select from the Tokyo Dawn Labs submenu?
questions.why: The screen shows a choice between 'TDR Kotelnikov' and 'TDR Nova', which serve different audio processing purposes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the specific audio processing tool that best fits the sound profile of your recording.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose between two plugins from the same maker - check which. They do different jobs, and one of them is not a compressor.
questions.check: which plugin was selected from the Tokyo Dawn Labs submenu, and is it actually a compressor
questions.say_example: Picked <TDR Kotelnikov>, the compressor. <TDR Nova> is a different tool.

questions.question: What does the meter read during the pauses, now that makeup gain is applied?
questions.why: Applying compression and make-up gain makes the quiet parts of the track louder, which can unintentionally amplify the background noise floor to an unacceptable level.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the subjective ear required to balance the benefits of a leveled voice against the drawback of amplified background noise.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied makeup gain after compression - listen to the pauses. Makeup gain lifts the silence between words as much as the words.
questions.check: what does the level meter read during a pause, after makeup gain was applied
questions.say_example: Heads up, the meter during pauses reads <-30 dB> now, up from <-48>. Makeup gain lifted the room noise too.

children.label: Apply a voice preset or profile

questions.question: Which specific audio segments do you want to apply the filter to?
questions.why: Selecting the exact audio regions in the workspace ensures the filter is only applied to the parts of the track that actually need processing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to use their own ear and judgment to decide exactly which clips require filtering.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied a voice treatment to some regions and not others - check which are covered. A filter on half the episode makes the speaker's voice change halfway through.
questions.check: which regions on the timeline have the filter applied, and which don't
questions.say_example: The filter's only on the first half of the track. The voice will change partway through.

questions.question: Which vocal filter should you apply to the audio?
questions.why: Cycling through the Voice filters in the Library pane and observing the changing Controls pane ensures you select the preset that best enhances the specific tonal qualities of the recording.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective ear required to listen to the looped playback and determine which vocal filter actually makes the speaker sound best.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a voice preset - check which one is highlighted. A narration preset is flat and close; a radio one is heavily coloured, and on a quiet recording it will bring the room up with the voice.
questions.check: which voice filter/preset is highlighted as selected
questions.say_example: Selected the <Narration> preset, not <Radio>. Radio would color a quiet recording more than it needs.

questions.question: Should you apply a generic voice profile or take the time to train a custom one?
questions.why: The Voice Profiler menu shows options to either apply a generic profile or learn a custom one, which determines how accurately the software enhances the specific speaker's voice.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether the audio requires a custom-trained voice profile for optimal quality or if a generic vocal boost is sufficient.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied a generic voice profile or trained one on this speaker - check which. A trained profile fits that voice; the generic one is a broadcast-sounding lift applied to anybody.
questions.check: was a generic voice profile applied, or a custom one trained on this speaker
questions.say_example: Trained a custom profile on this speaker instead of using the generic one.

questions.question: What target loudness and tolerance should you use to match the clips?
questions.why: The dialog requires specific parameters like a -23 LUFS target and 0.5 LU tolerance, which dictate the baseline volume of the speech segments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to customize the loudness standards to match the specific requirements of your podcast host or network.
questions.check: what loudness target and tolerance are set (e.g. -23 LUFS, 0.5 LU)
questions.say_example: Set the loudness target to <-23 LUFS>, so both clips match.

questions.question: What peak level is the normalize set to, and is DC offset being removed?
questions.why: The normalize dialog lets you set a specific peak amplitude, like -1.0 dB, and remove DC offset to ensure the waveform is centered and loud enough without clipping.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the control to set a custom peak amplitude target or decide if stereo channels should be normalized independently for this specific audio clip.
questions.verify_form: The agent normalised the audio to a peak - check the target. Minus one dB is the usual ceiling, and normalising to zero leaves no headroom for the mix.
questions.check: what peak amplitude is the normalize target set to, and is Remove DC Offset checked
questions.say_example: Normalized to <-1.0 dB>, not 0. Zero would leave no headroom for the mix.

questions.question: Do you want the software to automatically normalize the volume of the newly recorded audio?
questions.why: The waveform amplitude visibly decreased and the volume adjustment label dropped to -4.5 dB, showing that the software automatically matched the loudness of the existing track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to manually verify if the automatic volume reduction actually sounds balanced against the other voices in the mix.
questions.verify_form: The agent let the editor level the new recording automatically - check the result. It matches the loudness of what is already there, which is right only if what is already there is right.
questions.check: did auto-normalize change the new recording's level to match the existing track's loudness
questions.say_example: Auto-leveling dropped the new take by <4.5 dB> to match what's already there. That's only right if the existing track is right.

questions.question: Will you rely on the software's automatic leveling or manually adjust the clip volumes?
questions.why: The timeline shows the audio waveforms peaking right at the top due to the software's automatic leveling, meaning you must decide if this automated baseline is sufficient for your final mix.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the creative control of manually fine-tuning the volume dynamics to emphasize specific emotional moments in the speech.
questions.verify_form: The agent accepted the editor's automatic levels or set them itself - check which. Automatic levelling maximises loudness without clipping, and it flattens the moments you wanted loud.
questions.check: does the auto-leveled mix show peaks flattened to the same height across louder and quieter moments
questions.say_example: Auto-leveling maxed the volume across the board. The moment you wanted louder is now the same height as everything else.

questions.question: Did the software automatically adjust the volume of the music clip when you dropped it onto the timeline?
questions.why: Seeing the blue waveform's amplitude visibly decrease immediately upon placement confirms that the auto-leveling feature is active for imported media.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual reassurance of seeing the waveform shrink, which builds trust that the software's automated mixing tools are working correctly.
questions.check: did the music clip's level visibly drop on being placed on the timeline (auto-level on import)
questions.say_example: The music clip auto-leveled down on drop, from its original loudness.

questions.question: Is a section looping so the presets can be compared on the same words?
questions.why: Enabling the cycle tool in the top control bar to loop a specific region in the ruler area lets you hear how different filters affect the audio in real time.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally hear and evaluate how the applied filters change the nuances of the speaker's voice during continuous playback.
questions.check: is a loop/cycle region active over the comparison section
questions.say_example: Looped <0:14 to 0:18> to compare presets on the same words

questions.question: Was the previewed EQ curve applied to the whole track?
questions.why: Previewing the curve with its 100Hz drop-off and slight bass bump ensures the adjustment actually improves the voice's presence before committing to the change.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to use your own ears to judge whether the specific frequency adjustments actually flatter your unique voice.
questions.verify_form: The agent previewed an equaliser curve and applied it - check whether the change is one you would have kept. Applied to the whole track, this is on every word the speaker says.
questions.check: was the previewed EQ curve actually applied (committed) to the track, and what does the curve show (e.g. a 100Hz drop-off and a bass bump)
questions.say_example: Applied that curve to the whole track. Every word now has the <100Hz> drop-off and the bass lift, not just the preview section.

questions.question: Was the noise reduction written into the waveform, or added as an effect you can remove later?
questions.why: Applying an effect directly from the top menu permanently alters the underlying audio data, whereas using an effects rack allows you to tweak or remove the filter later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to easily reverse the audio cleaning later if you realize the noise reduction was too aggressive and degraded the voice quality.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied the cleanup destructively to the waveform or as a chain that can be switched off - check which. Destructive means the only way back is undo, and undo does not survive closing the project.
questions.check: was the noise reduction applied directly to the waveform (destructive), or through a real-time effects chain that can be removed later
questions.say_example: Applied that noise reduction straight to the waveform. Undo works now, but not after the project's closed and reopened.

questions.question: Is the loop tool still switched on?
questions.why: The highlighted loop icon in the control bar indicates that playback will continuously repeat a section, which disrupts the normal editing workflow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means losing the ability to quickly recognize and correct unintended playback settings that interrupt the flow of reviewing the audio.
questions.check: is the loop/cycle tool still toggled on
questions.say_example: Turned the loop tool back off

questions.question: Were the host's EQ and compressor settings copied onto the guest's track?
questions.why: The Mixer view shows the host channel has a populated effects block while the guest channel is empty, presenting an opportunity to duplicate the processing chain.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The creator loses the opportunity to evaluate whether the guest's unique voice actually requires the exact same EQ and compression as the host.
questions.verify_form: The agent copied the host's processing onto the guest's channel - check whether it suits that voice. Two people rarely need the same equalisation.
questions.check: were the host's EQ and dynamics settings copied directly onto the guest's channel
questions.say_example: Copied the host's EQ and compressor straight onto the guest's channel. Two different voices rarely want the same settings.

children.label: Cut the recording for content
children.note: 4.1 wherever the cut has to be made by eye. then 4.2 or 4.3 depending on whether the tool shows a waveform or a transcript. 4.4 then 4.5, or the two together, where highlighting and deleting happen as a single step. 4.6 does not come up when the action is a delete. 4.7 only in the transcript editor, and 4.8 is its bulk form. 4.9 after a cut that took too much, 4.10 after every cut, and 4.11 when it did not work. 4.12 where the missing words have to be replaced rather than closed over. 4.13 on the ends of the take, usually first.

questions.question: Is the whole recording in view, or only a scrolled-in part of it?
questions.why: The waveform was scrolling past the visible window, so clicking the zoom out button reveals the full scope of the track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual context of the episode's overall length and structure that comes from manually adjusting the timeline view.
questions.check: was the full waveform viewed at a zoomed-out scale before making cut decisions, or only a partially scrolled view
questions.say_example: Heads up, cuts were being marked from a scrolled-in view. Zooming out first so nothing off-screen gets missed.

questions.question: Should you highlight this unwanted noise spike for removal?
questions.why: Selecting the small spike in the bottom track's waveform isolates the distracting sound so it can be cleanly removed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the creative judgment to decide whether a specific vocal artifact adds character or is distracting enough to require manual deletion.
questions.verify_form: The agent marked a noise spike for removal - check what is inside the selection. A cough and a laugh look similar on a waveform, and one of them belongs in the episode.
questions.check: is the highlighted spike a noise sound or a natural vocal sound like a laugh
questions.say_example: Heads up, what's selected there looks like a laugh, not a noise spike. Check before it's cut.

questions.question: Is there a transcript, or are the filler words being found from the waveform alone?
questions.why: The timeline displays audio waveforms rather than a text transcript, making it harder to visually identify specific words to remove.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to personally review the spoken content to decide exactly which filler words and tangents should be cut.
questions.verify_form: The agent found filler words on a waveform with no transcript to read - check what it took out. Without the text, an um and the first sound of the next word look the same.
questions.check: is a transcript available, or is the filler word being identified purely from the waveform shape
questions.say_example: No transcript here, finding filler words by eye on the waveform alone. An 'um' and the start of the next word look the same.

questions.question: The speaker got a number wrong. Leave it in, cut it, or record a correction?
questions.why: The screen shows a buy price of $375 and a yearly rent price of $120, which contradicts the narrator's spoken claim that three years of renting equals the purchase price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: A person delegating to an agent loses the critical listening skills needed to catch and edit out a factual discrepancy in the spoken content.
questions.verify_form: The agent kept, cut or corrected the arithmetic mistake in the speech - check which. Leaving it in publishes a wrong figure; cutting it can leave the sentence unfinished.
questions.check: does the recording contain a factual/arithmetic error, and is the plan to cut it, leave it, or fix it with a new take
questions.say_example: The speaker's numbers are wrong here. <$99> a year isn't three years to <$249>. Leave the error in, cut it, or record a correction?

questions.question: Was this filler-word cut undone after it was tried?
questions.why: You deleted the highlighted text 'you know,' but immediately used the undo function because the resulting edit sounded too abrupt.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human ear's intuitive ability to judge whether removing a specific filler word ruins the natural cadence of the speaker's voice.
questions.verify_form: The agent removed a filler word - listen to the sentence without it. Some fillers carry the pause that makes the sentence land, and taking them out makes the speech abrupt.
questions.check: was this specific filler-word deletion undone after being tested
questions.say_example: Cut 'you know' there, then undid it. Without it, the line landed too abruptly.

questions.question: Which words should you remove as filler?
questions.why: Deleting the highlighted phrase ", you know," from the transcript text tightens the pacing of the spoken audio.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the editorial judgment of deciding whether a specific filler phrase disrupts the flow or adds natural conversational rhythm.
questions.verify_form: The agent deleted a filler phrase - check the sentence around it. Removing a phrase changes the rhythm even when it changes nothing else.
questions.check: which words are marked as filler for removal
questions.say_example: Marked <'like', 'you know', 'um'> for removal in this passage.

questions.question: Is the recording split at the points you want, into pieces you can move?
questions.why: Placing the Selection Tool at the 24-second mark and using the split menu command breaks the continuous recording into independent segments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the hands-on precision of choosing the exact millisecond to divide the clips for optimal pacing and natural transitions.
questions.verify_form: The agent split the recording at particular points - check where the boundaries are. A split a syllable early takes the front off the next word.
questions.check: where exactly does the split fall relative to the surrounding words
questions.say_example: Heads up, that split lands a syllable early. It'll take the front off the next word.

questions.question: Where do you place the playhead to make the first split?
questions.why: Positioning the playhead exactly at the 40-second mark before selecting the split command ensures you accurately target the beginning of the unwanted audio.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the editorial judgment of hearing the natural flow of speech to determine the exact millisecond where the mistake or tangent begins.
questions.verify_form: The agent placed the first cut point - check where. The start of the unwanted part is usually a breath earlier than it looks.
questions.check: where is the first cut boundary placed, relative to where the unwanted audio starts
questions.say_example: Placed the start cut at <0:40>. The unwanted part usually starts a breath earlier than it looks.

questions.question: Where should you place the playhead to mark the end of the unwanted section?
questions.why: Using the 'Split at Playhead' option at the exact timestamp ensures you isolate the unwanted audio without accidentally clipping the surrounding good take.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the editorial ear required to find the exact millisecond to cut so that the speaker's pacing and breath sound natural.
questions.verify_form: The agent placed the second cut point - check where. Cutting on the first sound of the next word is what makes an edit audible.
questions.check: where is the second cut boundary placed, relative to where the next word begins
questions.say_example: Placed the end cut right at the next word's first sound, that's what makes an edit audible. Pulling it back slightly.

questions.question: Is the unwanted speech isolated without the good audio either side of it?
questions.why: Using the right-click menu to split the highlighted waveform from 4.1 to 7.0 seconds ensures you precisely isolate the unwanted speech without deleting the surrounding content.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the editorial judgment of visually inspecting the waveform to place the exact split points that maintain a natural vocal cadence.
questions.verify_form: The agent isolated a stretch of speech to remove - check its edges. The good audio either side of it should still be there.
questions.check: does the isolated selection contain only the unwanted speech, with good audio intact on both sides
questions.say_example: The isolated span runs from <4.1s to 7.0s>. The good audio on either side is untouched.

questions.question: Is the selection on the audio itself rather than a loop region on the ruler?
questions.why: Clicking inside the clip selects the audio for editing, whereas clicking outside on the timeline ruler creates an unintended loop region.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the tactile awareness of exactly where to click on the interface to trigger a selection rather than a loop.
questions.check: is the current selection on the audio clip itself, or on the ruler (a loop region)
questions.say_example: Heads up, that's a loop region on the ruler, not a selection on the clip. Nothing will actually cut.

questions.question: Is only the voice track selected, or is the music selected too?
questions.why: The narrator explicitly warns to make sure only one track is selected before trimming, otherwise both the voice and music tracks will move in time simultaneously.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the awareness to check their track selection, risking unintended destructive edits to overlapping audio on other tracks.
questions.check: is only the intended track selected before trimming, or are both the voice and music tracks selected
questions.say_example: Heads up, both tracks are selected. Trimming now would move the music along with the voice.

questions.question: Is 'Snap-To' turned off, so cuts land where you put them?
questions.why: The bottom toolbar displays the 'Snap-To' option set to 'Off', which is crucial because enabling it would force your cursor to snap to grid lines or intervals, preventing you from making precise micro-cuts to remove breaths or subtle clicks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The awareness of a hidden timeline setting that, if accidentally enabled, fundamentally restricts the precision of all selection and cutting tools.
questions.check: is Snap-To turned off in the toolbar
questions.say_example: Snap-To is off, so cuts can land on the exact breath, not the nearest grid line.

questions.question: Which clip do you want to select on the timeline?
questions.why: Clicking a specific clip turns it gold, ensuring you are targeting the correct audio segment before making adjustments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the direct visual confirmation of knowing exactly which piece of audio is currently active for editing.
questions.check: which clip is selected on the timeline
questions.say_example: Selected the <interview> clip

questions.question: Is the unwanted stretch gone, and only that stretch?
questions.why: Activating the Selection Tool from the top toolbar allows you to precisely highlight and remove specific segments directly on the audio waveform.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually inspect the waveform and decide exactly where the boundaries of the cut should be.
questions.verify_form: The agent removed a stretch of the recording - check what is gone. The check is whether the speaker would still recognise what they said.
questions.check: what does the removed stretch contain, and is the sentence around it still complete
questions.say_example: Removed <3 seconds> there. The sentence on either side still reads as one complete thought.

questions.question: This span is something the speaker actually said. Keep it, or cut it?
questions.why: Deleting this isolated clip removes unwanted speech or silence from the timeline, directly shaping the pacing and narrative of the episode.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing your editorial judgment over whether that specific clip contained a valuable thought or just a distracting tangent.
questions.verify_form: The agent kept or discarded the piece it separated out - check what it was. A tangent to one person is the best part of the episode to another.
questions.check: what does the span about to be removed contain - a conclusion, a verdict, a caveat, a tangent, a story or an aside - rather than noise or filler
questions.say_example: That span is <a whole aside about how they got started>, not noise. Cutting it takes out something they actually said. Cut it, or keep it?

questions.question: Was the selected audio actually removed?
questions.why: The screen displayed a 'SUPR/RETROCESO' graphic, indicating the specific keyboard shortcuts required to remove the unwanted audio block.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the tactile control and speed of using their preferred keyboard shortcuts to instantly remove unwanted audio segments.
questions.check: was the selected audio removed
questions.say_example: Removed the selected span

questions.question: Is anything still selected that should not be before the cut is made?
questions.why: Knowing how to quickly clear active selections prevents you from accidentally deleting or altering the wrong audio clips on the multitrack timeline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the tactile control of rapidly testing and undoing specific cuts to ensure the pacing feels natural.
questions.check: is anything still selected elsewhere on the timeline before the delete key is pressed
questions.say_example: Heads up, another region further down is still selected too. Clearing that before deleting.

questions.question: Did the rest of the track stay where it was after that delete?
questions.why: Deleting the highlighted waveform directly causes the subsequent audio to shift left, so splitting the clip first preserves the timing of the rest of the track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether a specific cut should ripple the timeline or leave a gap to preserve overall synchronization.
questions.verify_form: The agent split around the piece before deleting it, or just deleted it - check whether everything after the cut moved. On a multi-speaker recording, moving one track and not the others puts the conversation out of sync for good.
questions.check: did the technique used (split-then-delete vs direct delete) leave the rest of this track shifted or in place
questions.say_example: Split around the clip before deleting it, so the timing of everything else on this track held.

questions.question: Did that delete close the gap, or leave one behind?
questions.why: The Edit menu offers both "Delete" and "Delete and Move", and choosing the latter automatically shifts the remaining audio left to close the empty space.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to learn efficient timeline management habits like ripple editing.
questions.verify_form: The agent used a delete that closes the gap, or one that leaves it - check the timeline. Closing it tightens the pace; leaving it keeps everything after in the same place.
questions.check: was Delete (leaves a gap) or Delete and Move (closes the gap) used
questions.say_example: Used Delete and Move, so the clips after it shifted earlier and the gap closed.

questions.question: Is the segment gone and the gap closed, with the two clips meeting cleanly?
questions.why: Deleting the selected clip and dragging the adjacent clip's title bar to snap them together prevents dead air and maintains a seamless audio flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually control the snapping behavior and visually verify that the pacing between the two joined clips feels natural.
questions.verify_form: The agent deleted the piece and pulled the next clip up to meet it - listen to the seam. Snapped together, two clips can leave a click or swallow a breath.
questions.check: do the two clips meet exactly at the join, with no overlap or gap left
questions.say_example: Heads up, dragging that clip left a sliver of silence at the join. Snapping it tighter.

questions.question: Did every speaker's track stay lined up after that cut?
questions.why: Deleting a section from one speaker's track without ripple-deleting the exact same duration from the other speakers' tracks will cause the rest of the conversation to be permanently out of sync.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The structural awareness to ensure edits are applied globally across a multitrack session to preserve conversational timing.
questions.check: did all the speaker tracks stay aligned with each other after this cut, or only the one that was edited
questions.say_example: Heads up, only this speaker's track shifted. The others are now out of sync with it.

children.label: Choose whether the words stay visible

questions.question: Should the filler words be struck through, or deleted outright?
questions.why: Using the strikethrough 'Ignore' option mutes the audio while leaving the text visible so you can track what was removed, whereas standard deletion removes the reference entirely.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the choice of keeping a visual record of the removed filler words in the transcript for future reference.
questions.verify_form: The agent deleted the filler words or struck them through - check the transcript. Struck through, the audio is cut and the text stays so you can see what went; deleted, both are gone.
questions.check: were the filler words struck through (Ignore, text stays visible) or fully deleted from the transcript
questions.say_example: Struck those words through instead of deleting them, so the text still shows what was cut.

questions.question: Which words stay in this line after the cuts?
questions.why: Testing different combinations of deletions and ignores in the transcript ensures the resulting audio edit sounds natural without losing the speaker's intent.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the editorial ear required to experiment with micro-edits and choose the exact combination of cuts that best preserves the speaker's natural cadence.
questions.verify_form: The agent worked through a sentence deleting and un-deleting words - check what survived. The result should still be something the speaker would recognise saying.
questions.check: After testing different delete/ignore combinations, which words remain in the final transcript?
questions.say_example: After trying a few combinations, kept everything except <'um', 'like'>. The line still reads as something they'd say.

questions.question: Which filler words were removed by hand instead of in the bulk pass?
questions.why: The transcript shows a cluster of filler words where automatic removal might sound unnatural, making a manual deletion necessary for a smoother edit.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the human ear required to judge exactly which filler words to cut while preserving a natural speaking cadence.
questions.verify_form: The agent removed some filler words by hand rather than with the bulk pass - check which ones. The bulk pass is even-handed and the manual one is a judgment about pacing.
questions.check: which filler words were removed by hand instead of through the bulk pass
questions.say_example: Removed <two> filler words by hand here instead of the bulk pass. The bulk pass would have cut the pause with them.

questions.question: Does the bulk removal tool's first count match the number in its confirmation?
questions.why: The discrepancy between the 868 filler words initially detected and the 368 shown in the confirmation popup suggests the tool might be missing a significant portion of the edits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to catch this software discrepancy and manually verify if the remaining 500 filler words were actually removed.
questions.check: does the bulk-removal tool's initial count of filler words match the count shown in its confirmation popup
questions.say_example: The tool found <868> filler words at first. The confirmation only lists <368>. The rest aren't accounted for.

children.label: Repair a cut that took too much

questions.question: Does the waveform at the automated cut show a clipped edge, or a natural taper?
questions.why: The timeline shows the ignored filler word as a blue section, which matters because automated cuts can be too aggressive and clip the waveform of the next word.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the human ear's ability to judge the micro-timing of speech and ensure the edit sounds perfectly natural.
questions.verify_form: The agent made a text-driven cut - listen to it. A cut taken from the transcript often clips the head of the next word, and the fix is to drag the boundary back.
questions.check: does the waveform show a clipped, abrupt edge at the automated cut boundary, or a natural taper
questions.say_example: Heads up, that automated cut clips right into the next word's waveform. Dragging the boundary back a touch.

questions.question: Where exactly should you drag the clip boundary to fine-tune this edit?
questions.why: Adjusting the edge of the audio waveform in the timeline provides precise control over the cut, ensuring no breath or syllable is unnaturally clipped.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ear to judge the natural pacing and rhythm of the spoken transition.
questions.verify_form: The agent dragged the clip boundary to fine-tune the cut - check where it landed. A syllable either way is the difference between speech and a stutter.
questions.check: where does the dragged clip boundary land relative to the word it's trimming
questions.say_example: Dragged the boundary to <0:42.1>. A syllable either way and this reads as a stutter.

questions.question: Is the cut on a zero-crossing, or will it click?
questions.why: Splicing audio waveforms at a point other than the zero-amplitude line creates a sudden jump in the signal, which the listener hears as a sharp digital click.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the technical precision of ensuring every edit is clean and artifact-free at the microscopic waveform level.
questions.check: does the cut point align with a zero-crossing on the waveform
questions.say_example: Heads up, that cut isn't on a zero-crossing. It'll click. Nudging it a few samples.

questions.question: Should you play back the end of this region to check the context?
questions.why: Hearing the final words of the region helps determine exactly where the next audio segment should begin to maintain a natural flow.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the intuitive human ear for pacing and conversational context when bridging two separate audio takes.
questions.verify_form: The agent played the end of the region before joining the next one - check that it did. The words either side of a join decide whether it sounds like a conversation.
questions.check: was the end of the region played back before the next segment begins
questions.say_example: Played back the end of that region

questions.question: Does the waveform at the cut edge show half a breath?
questions.why: Slicing exactly at the start of a word often cuts a natural breath in half, making the speaker sound like a machine and jarring the listener.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The intuitive understanding of human speech rhythms and the need for natural breathing space between thoughts.
questions.verify_form: The agent cut close to a word - listen for the breath. Half a breath left in sounds worse than the whole one, and none at all sounds mechanical.
questions.check: does the waveform at the cut edge show a truncated or partial breath shape
questions.say_example: Heads up, the waveform right at that cut shows half a breath. Either extend it or take the rest with it.

children.label: Undo the cut and try again

questions.question: Can the edit be undone and redone so you can hear it both ways?
questions.why: The toolbar's undo and redo arrows let you instantly restore a cut portion of the audio to check your work before removing it again.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to quickly toggle an edit on and off to hear the difference and verify the cut was made in exactly the right spot.
questions.check: was undo/redo used to compare the cut both ways
questions.say_example: Toggled undo and redo to compare the cut both ways

children.label: Patch the hole with another take

questions.question: Does the patch come from the same take as the audio around it?
questions.why: Splitting the clip boundaries and using the time shift tool allows you to precisely remove a coughing fit and insert replacement audio without disrupting the track's overall timing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective judgment required to hear whether the pasted replacement clip blends naturally into the surrounding dialogue.
questions.verify_form: The agent replaced a stretch with other audio - listen across the join. A pasted replacement carries its own room tone and its own pace, and both are audible.
questions.check: does the replacement clip come from a different take or file than the surrounding audio
questions.say_example: The patch here is from <a different take>, recorded on another day. It'll carry its own room tone.

questions.question: Should you duplicate this section of audio instead of deleting it?
questions.why: The toolbar displays undo, copy, and paste buttons that allow you to recover and replicate the segment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative discretion to realize a specific audio clip is worth repurposing elsewhere in the episode rather than discarding it.
questions.verify_form: The agent copied a section rather than deleting it - check what it kept. Some cut audio is worth reusing elsewhere in the episode.
questions.check: was the section copied and kept, rather than deleted outright
questions.say_example: Copied that section instead of deleting it. Might reuse it later in the episode.

questions.question: What did the trim at the end of the track take with it?
questions.why: Using the selection tool to highlight and delete the end of the top track ensures that unwanted extra audio is cleanly removed from the timeline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment of determining exactly where the natural conversation ends and which trailing audio should be cut.
questions.verify_form: The agent removed audio from the end of the take - check what went. There is usually silence and chair noise there, and sometimes the last thing the speaker said.
questions.check: what does the trimmed portion at the end of the track actually contain
questions.say_example: Heads up, the trimmed end included the speaker's last sentence, not just chair noise. Check before this is final.

questions.question: Is the cursor on the trim half of that edge, or the loop half?
questions.why: The cursor changes to a loop tool on the upper half of the edge and a trim tool on the lower half, determining how the region behaves when dragged.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual feedback of the cursor changing and the precise control over dragging the trim tool to the exact desired length.
questions.check: is the cursor on the lower half of the region's edge (trim) or the upper half (loop) before dragging
questions.say_example: Cursor's on the loop half of that edge. Dropping to the lower half so dragging trims instead of loops.

questions.question: Is the end of the episode where you want it?
questions.why: Playing back the timeline from the beginning lets you verify the audio quality and identify the exact timestamp to end the cut.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment required to listen to the flow of the conversation and decide exactly where the episode should naturally conclude.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose where the episode stops - check the last thing that is in it. What sounds like an ending in the room is often a false one on the recording.
questions.check: what is the last clip or word at the very end of the timeline
questions.say_example: The episode now ends on <'...and that's the show'>, not the earlier false ending.

questions.question: Does the trimmed start of the episode sit right against the end of the intro?
questions.why: Trimming the orange audio region to the 35-second mark and dragging it to abut the purple intro region ensures the main content begins smoothly without dead air.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing creative control over the exact pacing and timing of the transition between the intro and the main episode.
questions.verify_form: The agent trimmed the head of the episode audio and butted it against the intro - check where it starts. The first words matter more than any other cut in the episode.
questions.check: where does the trimmed head of the episode sit relative to where the intro region ends
questions.say_example: Trimmed the start to <0:35> and butted it right against the intro's end. No dead air between them.

children.label: Arrange the episode
children.note: 5.1 decides the running order, and in three keepers the order is a track layout rather than a sequence. 5.2 does most of the moving; 5.3 where a piece belongs on a different track; 5.4 and 5.5 adjust where the pieces meet. 5.6 has to be redone after almost every move in the GarageBand runs. 5.7 once the whole thing exists.

children.label: Set the order of the segments

questions.question: Should you place each distinct segment on its own dedicated track?
questions.why: The zoomed-out workspace shows audio regions placed sequentially from left to right across multiple named tracks, which allows for independent volume adjustments for each unique element.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to organize the timeline structure in a way that makes sense for your personal editing and mixing workflow.
questions.verify_form: The agent put each segment on its own track or stacked them on one - check the layout. One per track means each keeps its own level; one track means one level for everything.
questions.check: is each segment on its own track, or stacked together on one track
questions.say_example: Each segment has its own track, so each keeps its own level.

questions.question: Does the interview start right where the audio tag ends?
questions.why: Aligning the [name] and [name] audio regions exactly at the end of the 'Audio Tag' region ensures the interview begins seamlessly after the intro.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to visually verify that the interview tracks are perfectly synchronized with each other and properly sequenced after the intro tag.
questions.check: does the interview audio start exactly where the Audio Tag region ends
questions.say_example: Lined the interview up right at the end of the audio tag, so it starts without a gap.

questions.question: Did shortening this clip to fit take part of a word, or only trailing silence?
questions.why: Dragging the right edge of the purple audio region ensures the female voice track aligns correctly on the timeline without overlapping the next segment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to fine-tune the exact pacing and conversational flow between segments.
questions.verify_form: The agent shortened the last clip to fit - check what came off. A clip trimmed to fit the timeline can lose the end of a sentence.
questions.check: does the trimmed edge of the shortened clip cut into spoken words, and how much speech does it take, rather than only trailing silence
questions.say_example: The trim on the <outro> clip took the end of a word, not just the silence after it.

questions.question: Is the clip being treated as the main episode the one labeled as the outro?
questions.why: You identified the purple clip as the actual episode, but visual evidence from earlier in the session showed this specific clip being recorded as the outro.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent can accurately track the identity and purpose of specific audio clips throughout a complex editing session.
questions.check: does the clip's track name or region label identify it as the outro rather than the main episode
questions.say_example: The clip being treated as the episode is the one labeled <outro>.

children.label: Move a segment along the timeline

questions.question: How much space should you leave at the beginning of the timeline for the new intro?
questions.why: Dragging the 'Audio Tag' region to the 44-second mark ensures there is enough empty space on the timeline to insert the introductory segment without overlapping existing audio.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control over the exact pacing and breathing room between the intro and the start of the main audio.
questions.verify_form: The agent made room at the front of the timeline - check how much. That space is what the intro has to fit into.
questions.check: does the empty space left at the front of the timeline match or exceed the length of the intro file being inserted
questions.say_example: There's <12> seconds open at the front, but the intro file runs <18>.

questions.question: Is the shift tool active rather than a tool that would trim the clip?
questions.why: The screen shows a selection made on the top track followed by choosing the Time Shift Tool, which contradicts the draft's claim that a trim action occurred.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to visually verify that the correct tool was selected to shift the audio rather than accidentally trimming it.
questions.check: does the toolbar show the Time Shift Tool selected rather than a trim tool
questions.say_example: The tool selected there moves audio, it doesn't trim it.
