questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The creator loses their preferred visual organization of the workspace, which helps them quickly identify tracks at a glance.
questions.verify_form: The agent ordered the speaker layers - check which is on top. The top layer is the one that covers the others when the layouts overlap.
questions.check: is the host's layer positioned above the guests' in the layer stack
questions.say_example: The <guest>'s layer sits above the host's in the stack.

questions.question: Which visual template and layout should you apply to the scene?
questions.why: The template browser displays various color themes like Cool Gray and Burgundy alongside layouts for one to four people, dictating the visual branding of the episode.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means you lose the ability to match the visual aesthetic and speaker layout to your specific brand and recording.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied a visual template and a speaker layout - check both. The colourway is your show's branding and the layout has to match the number of people talking.
questions.check: does the applied color theme match the show's standard branding, and does the layout match the number of speakers in the scene
questions.say_example: The layout picked fits <2> people, but there are <3> speakers in this scene.

questions.question: Should you apply a pre-built multi-camera template to this scene?
questions.why: The template gallery displays options like 'Picture in Picture' and 'Fullscreen Two Camera' that can automatically format your video layout.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether a pre-built layout fits your show's aesthetic or if a custom design is needed.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied a built-in multi-camera layout or built one - check which. The built-in ones are quick and they look like everybody else's.
questions.check: was a pre-built multi-camera template applied, per the template panel, or was a custom layout built
questions.say_example: Applied the built-in <Picture in Picture> template

questions.question: Do you need to adjust the crop and zoom to fix the speaker's headroom?
questions.why: The crop tool overlay and zoom control showed the speaker had too much headroom, requiring a zoom adjustment to 116% and repositioning for a better visual layout.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose your personal aesthetic judgment on how tightly framed and positioned a speaker should be for the best visual impact.
questions.verify_form: The agent cropped and zoomed a speaker's frame - check the headroom. Too much space above the head and the shot looks accidental; too little and the head is cut off.
questions.check: does the speaker's framing show excess space above the head, or is the head cropped at the frame edge
questions.say_example: The zoom is at <95%>, leaving a lot of empty space above <the guest's> head.

questions.question: Should the layout automatically switch to the active speaker?
questions.why: The 'Multi-cam' dropdown in the layout properties panel lets you choose whether to lock the video to a specific person or dynamically switch to whoever is talking.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose creative control over the visual focus, as an agent might strictly follow the active speaker rather than intentionally showing another speaker's reaction.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the layout to follow whoever is speaking, or locked it to one person - check which. Following the speaker is the default and it misses reactions.
questions.check: is the multi-cam mode set to follow the active speaker or locked to one person, per the dropdown
questions.say_example: Set to follow whoever is speaking

questions.question: Which camera angle do you want to display in this layout box?
questions.why: The 'Multi-cam' dropdown allows you to override the default active speaker view and lock a specific person's camera feed to a layout box.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control to manually highlight specific visual reactions or speakers during the conversation.
questions.verify_form: The agent assigned a camera feed to a layout box - check which. A box locked to a silent person is a long shot of somebody listening.
questions.check: does the camera feed assigned to this layout box match the speaker who is actually talking at that point
questions.say_example: That box is locked to <a guest> who isn't speaking in this stretch.

children.label: Fill the canvas with one speaker

questions.question: Is the speaker filling the screen the one who's talking?
questions.why: The canvas currently displays a 3-up video layout, and using the Position dropdown alongside the Layers panel allows you to isolate the active speaker visually without deleting the other tracks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control to decide exactly which speaker to visually highlight and when to transition away from the multi-person gallery view.
questions.verify_form: The agent made one speaker fill the screen and hid the others - check who is on screen. That is a deliberate choice about who the moment belongs to.
questions.check: is the speaker shown full-screen the one who is actually speaking at that point in the transcript
questions.say_example: The speaker shown full-screen is <the host>, but <the guest> is talking at this point.

questions.question: Where should you start the next scene to apply a different layout?
questions.why: Typing a slash before a specific paragraph in the transcript creates a scene boundary so the new visual layout aligns perfectly with the shift in topic.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative intuition of timing visual layout changes to match the natural rhythm and emphasis of the speaker's delivery.
questions.verify_form: The agent started a new scene at a particular point in the transcript - check where. That is where the picture changes, so it should land on a change of subject.
questions.check: does the new scene boundary fall at a point where the topic changes in the transcript, rather than mid-thought
questions.say_example: The new scene starts mid-sentence, not at a change of subject.

questions.question: Was the layout copied to the other scenes, or the template re-applied over them?
questions.why: The Scene panel reveals options to copy and paste layouts, allowing you to efficiently standardize the configuration across multiple segments without manual rework.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to selectively apply your preferred layout to specific scenes to maintain creative control over the episode's flow.
questions.verify_form: The agent copied a layout to the other scenes or re-applied the template - check the framing. Re-applying the template throws away the crops you set.
questions.check: was the layout copied over, preserving the crops already set, or was the template re-applied, resetting them
questions.say_example: The template was re-applied there, which reset the crop and zoom already set for <the guest>.

questions.question: Do the visual clips line up with the passages of speech they illustrate?
questions.why: Layering video clips above the main track to align with highlighted transcript phrases provides necessary visual context for the audience.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative judgment of deciding exactly which video clips best enhance the specific phrases being spoken.
questions.verify_form: The agent laid visual clips over particular passages of speech - check the alignment. B-roll a sentence late illustrates the wrong point.
questions.check: does the visual clip's start time align with the transcript passage it's meant to illustrate
questions.say_example: That clip starts <5>s after the line it's meant to illustrate.

children.label: Set the levels
children.note: 7.1 whenever the meters are visible; it is what sends the user to 7.2 or 7.3. 7.2 for a whole track and 7.3 for one clip. 7.4 whenever music runs under speech, and it has to be redone if 5 or 6 moves anything. 7.5 at every seam. 7.6 in a multi-speaker episode. 7.7 once the parts are balanced against each other, and 7.8 where the level is read off a meter instead of judged by ear. 7.9 after any of them.

questions.question: Should you use the track volume slider to fade the music under the voice?
questions.why: The track volume slider applies a static volume change to the entire track, meaning it cannot be used to lower the music only when the voice starts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to dictate the exact timing and depth of the music fades that make room for the spoken dialogue.
questions.verify_form: The agent used the track's static level control to try to duck the music - check the result. A static level cannot come down only while the voice is speaking, so either the music is too loud under the voice or too quiet on its own.
questions.check: was a static track volume change used to try to lower the music only during speech, rather than automation or an auto-duck effect
questions.say_example: That's a flat volume drop on the whole track, so the music is either too loud under the host or too quiet on its own.

questions.question: Are your audio levels staying out of the red zone on the meters?
questions.why: Watching the track meters stay in the green and yellow ensures the audio won't clip and become distorted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual confirmation that the dynamic range of the conversation is safely contained without harsh clipping.
questions.check: does any track's meter show levels reaching into the red or clipping zone
questions.say_example: The <guest> track's meter is hitting red.

questions.question: Is the master output meter clipping when the host, guest, and music all play simultaneously?
questions.why: Even if individual tracks are safely in the green, summing them together at a transition point can overload the master bus and cause distortion.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The holistic awareness to check the master bus levels during the busiest parts of the mix, not just individual track levels.
questions.check: does the master or output meter clip when all tracks play together, even if individual tracks read safely
questions.say_example: Each track reads fine alone, but the master meter clips when they all play together.

questions.question: Is the clip light lit at the top of the master meter?
questions.why: Audio editors leave a sticky red dot at the top of the meter if the audio clips even once, serving as a visual warning long after the loud moment has passed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The visual safety net that flags momentary distortion, which might be missed by ear or if the person looks away during playback.
questions.check: is the sticky clip indicator lit at the top of the master meter, showing a clip occurred at some point
questions.say_example: The clip light at the top of the master meter is lit, from a peak somewhere in the mix.

questions.question: Should you adjust the stereo panning for the tracks?
questions.why: The L and R pan sliders on the track headers control the stereo placement of the audio, which is a stylistic choice even if typically unnecessary for standard podcasts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative choice to experiment with spatial audio separation for your speakers.
questions.verify_form: The agent panned the tracks or left them centred - check the pan controls. For a podcast centred is normal, and panned speakers put one person in one ear.
questions.check: are the L or R pan sliders set away from center on the voice tracks
questions.say_example: The <host> track is panned <full left>. That voice will only play in one ear.

questions.question: What gain level should you set for the background music track?
questions.why: Watching the tooltip values drop to -16.0 dB as you drag the slider ensures the music waveform is visually and audibly reduced so it doesn't overpower the voice tracks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ears to balance the emotional impact of the music against the clarity of the spoken dialogue.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the music bed's level - check the number. Around -16 dB under a voice is usual; a few dB either way is the difference between a bed and a distraction.
questions.check: what is the music track's gain level in dB, relative to the voice tracks
questions.say_example: The music bed sits <4> dB under the voice. The usual for a bed is more like <16> dB under.

questions.question: How much should you adjust the volume of this specific track?
questions.why: The volume slider on the track header lets you compensate for soft audio so the interview matches the rest of the mix.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ears to decide exactly how much of a volume boost the interview needs to sound natural alongside the other tracks.
questions.verify_form: The agent changed this track's level - check the number against the others. A quiet interview lifted too far brings its room up with it.
questions.check: does this track's level now sit close to the other tracks' levels, or still noticeably off
questions.say_example: This track is still reading <6> dB quieter than the others after the adjustment.

questions.question: Does this track read louder than the rest of the mix?
questions.why: The playback meter bouncing into the yellow zone indicates the track is slightly too loud and needs to be turned down to match the rest of the mix.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective judgment of hearing how the voices sit together and deciding exactly how much to manually attenuate the track.
questions.verify_form: The agent adjusted a track that sat too loud - check where it ended up. Matching by eye on the waveform and matching by ear are not the same thing.
questions.check: does this track's meter read noticeably louder, such as into yellow, compared to the rest of the mix
questions.say_example: This track peaks in yellow while the rest of the mix sits in green.

questions.question: Does the music bed show the level reduction that was asked for?
questions.why: The narrator stated they would lower the music bed's volume, which is confirmed by the application of a -2.7 dB Amplification effect on that track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent followed through on their spoken intention to properly mix the background music.
questions.check: does a gain or amplification effect show a reduction applied to the music bed track, against the reduction that was asked for
questions.say_example: The music bed shows no gain reduction applied, though you asked for it to come down.

questions.question: Is the intro's level and stereo position set against the rest of the mix?
questions.why: The track header displays volume, pan, mute, and solo controls that are essential for balancing the intro against the rest of the mix.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually audition the track and fine-tune its exact volume and stereo placement to match your creative preference.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the intro's level and stereo position - check both against the rest of the mix. An intro louder than the episode makes listeners reach for the volume twice.
questions.check: is the intro track's volume noticeably louder than the rest of the mix, per the track header's level and pan controls
questions.say_example: The intro is <5> dB above the rest of the mix. It'll jump out when the episode starts.

questions.question: How much can this be lifted before it clips?
questions.why: The software disabled the OK button when the new peak amplitude exceeded 0.0 dB, ensuring you do not accidentally distort the track.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide exactly how close to the maximum safe volume threshold you want to push this specific segment.
questions.check: does the resulting peak amplitude after amplification stay at or below 0 dB
questions.say_example: Amplifying by <+4> dB would push the peak to <+1.2> dB. That's over the ceiling.

questions.question: How much should you pull down the volume envelope for this specific section?
questions.why: Adjusting the blue envelope line ensures this specific waveform visually and audibly matches the surrounding audio so the speaker doesn't sound jarringly loud.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective, ear-driven judgment of exactly how much to attenuate a specific phrase to make it sound natural in context.
questions.verify_form: The agent pulled one phrase down with the envelope - check how far. A phrase levelled flat against its neighbours takes the emphasis out of it.
questions.check: does the pulled-down section's level now sit flush with its neighbors rather than clearly standing out
questions.say_example: That section is still reading <3> dB louder than the lines around it.

questions.question: Do the two Amplify dialogs report the same original peak for the same selection?
questions.why: Calculating the original peak amplitude of -0.8375 dB from both the 3.0 dB and 0.4 dB amplification dialogs confirms the software is consistently reading the selection's levels.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to mathematically cross-check the software's level readings to ensure the underlying audio remains consistent between adjustments.
questions.check: does the original peak amplitude reported in one Amplify dialog match the value reported in another dialog for the same selection
questions.say_example: One Amplify dialog reads the original peak as <-0.84> dB and the other as <-1.1> dB, for the same selection.

questions.question: How much should you lower the volume of this clip?
questions.why: Dragging the node at the top center of the clip adjusts its overall volume so it balances properly with the rest of the mix.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to use your own ears to decide exactly how loud this specific segment should be relative to the other tracks.
questions.verify_form: The agent lowered the whole clip's level - check the number. This moves everything in the clip, including the quiet parts you may have wanted to keep quiet.
questions.check: did lowering the clip's overall volume also pull down a part that was already at the right level
questions.say_example: That drop also pulled the quieter part of the clip down further, not just the loud part.

questions.question: Do the relative and absolute numbers in the tooltip add up?
questions.why: Checking that the absolute volume and relative change values in the tooltips mathematically align confirms the editor is accurately tracking the clip's original -12.5 dB baseline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to manually verify that the software's volume adjustments are mathematically consistent across different edits.
questions.check: does the relative change shown, applied to the clip's original baseline, equal the absolute value shown in the tooltip
questions.say_example: The tooltip says <+3> dB from a <-12.5> dB baseline, then reports <-8> dB absolute. Those don't add up.

questions.question: Is the Multi-tool the one active in the toolbar?
questions.why: Selecting the Multi-tool (asterisk icon) combines the functions of the Selection and Envelope tools, allowing you to highlight audio and adjust volume curves without constantly switching tools in the toolbar.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the hands-on efficiency of using a combined tool to speed up your manual volume adjustments and edits.
questions.verify_form: The agent switched to a combined selection and level tool - check the toolbar. It saves swapping tools and it also makes an accidental drag change a level.
questions.check: is the Multi-tool the one currently active in the toolbar
questions.say_example: Switched to the Multi-tool

questions.question: Was the boost applied with the Amplify effect, or the Envelope tool?
questions.why: While the Amplify effect works, the narrator notes a preference for the Envelope tool because it provides continuous visual feedback on exactly how much the track is being boosted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The opportunity to choose a volume adjustment tool that provides better visual feedback, which helps build an intuitive understanding of audio levels.
questions.verify_form: The agent used an amplify effect or the envelope to lift the track - check which. The envelope shows the amount as you drag it; the effect applies it and leaves no trace.
questions.check: was the boost applied via the Amplify effect or the Envelope tool
questions.say_example: Boosted using the Amplify effect

children.label: Duck the music under the voice
children.note: 7.4.1 in most keepers, drawn against the speech on the track above. 7.4.2 where the tool offers to do it, and it needs 7.4.3 first because the effect reads the track underneath as its control. 7.4.4 where the change is applied to a selection instead of drawn as a curve. 7.4.5 after any of them, and in DtmO it sends the work back twice.

questions.question: Will you use auto-ducking or manual envelope adjustments to lower the background music?
questions.why: The visible waveforms indicate the music track's amplitude is too high and will overpower the spoken words if not reduced.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative choice of deciding whether an automated ducking effect sounds natural enough or if the track requires precise manual fading.
questions.verify_form: The agent ducked the music automatically or drew the level by hand - check which. The automatic pass is even and it does not follow a clip that moves afterwards.
questions.check: was the music lowered via an Auto Duck effect or via manually drawn envelope points
questions.say_example: Used Auto Duck to lower the music

questions.question: Where do you place the control points to taper off the track's volume?
questions.why: Dragging the control points on the waveform's gray envelope bars determines exactly when and how smoothly the audio fades out.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to listen to the playback and subjectively decide if the timing and slope of the fade-out feel natural.
questions.verify_form: The agent drew control points to taper the level - check where they sit. The slope decides whether the change is heard as a fade or as a step.
questions.check: are there at least two spaced-out control points forming a slope, rather than a single point making a step
questions.say_example: There's only one control point there. That makes a sudden step rather than a taper.

questions.question: Where should you place the automation points to duck the music under the intro?
questions.why: Setting precise automation points on the timeline ensures the music fades smoothly to a lower decibel level exactly as the spoken narration begins.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to fine-tune the pacing and emotional feel of the audio transition between the theme music and the host's voice.
questions.verify_form: The agent placed automation points to duck the music under the narration - check where they land against the first and last words. Late and the music covers the opening.
questions.check: does the first automation point, where the music starts ducking, fall at or before the first spoken word of the intro
questions.say_example: The first duck point lands <1.5>s after the intro's first word. The music covers the opening line.

questions.question: Is the automation curve smooth, or does it step sharply between points?
questions.why: Drawing automation can create uneven points; a sighted user can easily see if the curve looks smooth or erratic.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might generate an automation envelope that mathematically achieves the target volume but visually looks (and audibly sounds) jagged and unnatural.
questions.check: does the drawn automation curve show smooth transitions between points, or sharp stair-step jumps
questions.say_example: The curve has a hard stair-step jump around <the second verse>, not a smooth ramp.

questions.question: How steeply should the music fade out when the voice track begins?
questions.why: The screen shows the music track overlapping the voice track, meaning the music's volume must be ducked using the envelope tool so the narration remains clear.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses personal control over the exact timing and dramatic feel of the music fading under their vocal delivery.
questions.verify_form: The agent set how steeply the music drops as the voice starts - check the slope. A steep drop is heard as a cut; a slow one leaves the music over the first sentence.
questions.check: how many seconds does the duck take to reach its low point once the voice begins
questions.say_example: The duck takes <3.5>s to come down. The first sentence plays over full music.

questions.question: Where should you place the envelope points to fade in the music after the voiceover?
questions.why: The visual placement of control points on the music waveform dictates the exact timing and dramatic effect of the volume swell.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to subjectively time the music's emotional swell to match the pacing and tone of the final spoken words.
questions.verify_form: The agent brought the music back up after the voice - check where. Too early and it steps on the last words.
questions.check: does the music's fade-in point begin at or after the end of the voiceover's last word
questions.say_example: The music starts climbing back up <0.4>s before the last word finishes.

questions.question: What duck amount and fade times is Auto Duck set to?
questions.why: Moving the music track to the top and applying specific Auto Duck values like a -11.4 dB duck amount and 0.50-second fades ensures the music dips smoothly around the dialogue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose control over the exact fade timings and volume thresholds that determine how naturally the music ducks under the voices.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the automatic ducking - check the duck amount and the fade times. Around -12 dB with half-second fades is usual; deeper or faster is heard as pumping.
questions.check: what duck amount in dB and what fade times in seconds are set in the Auto Duck dialog
questions.say_example: Auto Duck is set to <-20> dB with <0.1>s fades. That's deep and fast enough to sound like pumping.

children.label: Order the tracks for the effect

questions.question: Is the music track at the top of the stack, with Auto Duck applied?
questions.why: The screen shows the music track being repositioned and the effect applied to ensure the music volume drops appropriately during spoken segments.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to fine-tune the specific threshold and fade parameters of the ducking effect to match their desired audio aesthetic.
questions.check: does the track order show the music track at the top, and does it have the Auto Duck effect applied
questions.say_example: The music track is still <third> in the list, and no Auto Duck effect shows applied.

questions.question: Does the duck cover the whole line, and is the music low enough under it?
questions.why: The timeline shows the newly added '[music file]' clip overlapping with 'Interview 2', requiring a specific volume reduction on the music track so it doesn't overpower the speech.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user surrenders the aesthetic judgment of exactly how loud the background music should be relative to the speaker's voice to set the right mood.
questions.verify_form: The agent set where and how far the music ducks - check both. The depth is the balance and the bounds are the timing.
questions.check: does the ducked span's start and end align with the actual speech, and is the ducked level low enough that the voice isn't masked
questions.say_example: The duck only covers part of the line. The music comes back up while <the guest> is still talking.

questions.question: Does the hand-drawn envelope drop low enough, and does it line up with the dialogue?
questions.why: The visible decibel tooltips on the yellow volume envelope show that the music's fade slopes and floor levels need precise tuning to sit properly under the speech.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might just apply a default ducking algorithm, losing the human editor's ear for timing the fades and crafting stylistic endings like an infinite fade.
questions.verify_form: The agent shaped the ducking envelope by hand - check the slopes and the floor. This is where a long tail or an abrupt drop gets decided.
questions.check: does the envelope's floor level and slope timing align with the start and end of the dialogue it's meant to duck under
questions.say_example: The envelope floor sits at <-6> dB, still audible over quieter dialogue.

children.label: Check the duck against the speech

questions.question: Do the Auto Duck dips still line up with the voice clip after it moved?
questions.why: The screen showed the volume dips on the music track remaining in their original positions after the audio clip was moved, indicating the effect does not update dynamically.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the contextual awareness to realize the music ducking is now out of sync with the vocals, resulting in awkward background music volume drops during silence.
questions.check: After the voice clip was moved, do the Auto Duck dips on the music track still align with the clip's new position, or remain at the old position?
questions.say_example: The duck dips are still lined up with where the clip used to be, not where it is now.

questions.question: Is the hand-drawn fade curve smooth, or jagged?
questions.why: The manual envelope points created a visibly uneven volume curve on the waveform, prompting a switch to a cleaner preset effect.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the subjective auditory judgment to recognize a clunky manual fade and the preference to replace it with a smoother preset.
questions.verify_form: The agent kept a hand-drawn fade or replaced it with the menu fade - check which. The hand-drawn one can be shaped and it can also come out uneven.
questions.check: does the manually drawn envelope curve show smooth transitions, or a visibly jagged, uneven shape
questions.say_example: The hand-drawn curve has a jagged jump around <0:42> instead of a smooth taper.

questions.question: Does the music swell back up during a pause inside someone's sentence?
questions.why: The waveform visually indicates that the music volume swells up inappropriately because it detects a pause in the narration.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might trust the automated ducking feature without realizing it creates a jarring volume jump during a brief silence.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied automatic ducking - listen to the gaps in the speech. Ducking reads silence as room to swell back up, and a brief pause becomes a volume jump.
questions.check: does the ducked music level rise back up during a pause within a single speaker's dialogue, before that speaker resumes
questions.say_example: The music swells back up during a <1.2>s pause mid-sentence, then ducks again once talking resumes.

children.label: Fade a clip in or out

questions.question: How do you want to fade in the start of the trimmed clip?
questions.why: The fade handle and its tooltip options for duration and shape determine how smoothly the volume ramps up to prevent abrupt clicks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually adjust the fade curve and timing by ear to perfectly match the natural rhythm of the speaker's entry.
questions.verify_form: The agent put a fade on the start of the clip - check its length. Too short and there is a click; too long and the first word is swallowed.
questions.check: how long is the fade-in applied at the start of the clip
questions.say_example: The fade-in there runs <400>ms, long enough to swallow the first word.

questions.question: Does the clip fade in at the start, or jump straight to full?
questions.why: Checking the visual reduction and gradual increase in the waveform confirms the fade-in effect was applied successfully to prevent an abrupt start.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to visually verify that the fade's slope and duration match your desired pacing for the audio.
questions.check: does the waveform at the clip's start show a gradually increasing shape, or does it start at full amplitude immediately
questions.say_example: The waveform jumps straight to full height at the start. There's no fade on it.

questions.question: Does the waveform show the fade-down that was applied?
questions.why: The narrator claims the track fades down, but the visual waveform of the bottom track does not show any volume reduction effect applied after the initial fade-in.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the intended audio mix because the agent fails to actually apply the necessary volume reduction to the track.
questions.check: does the music track's waveform show any amplitude reduction after the point the fade was applied
questions.say_example: The waveform there stays flat. No fade-down shows after that point.

questions.question: Which effect should you apply to the selected audio?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Efecto' menu with various processing options, and selecting 'Desvanecer progresivamente' applies a smooth volume fade out to the clip.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control to decide exactly how and when the audio volume should taper off for stylistic effect.
questions.verify_form: The agent applied a fade effect to the selection - check which direction and how far it reaches. A fade applied to the wrong end does the opposite of what was wanted.
questions.check: does the applied effect match a fade-out, decreasing toward the end, rather than a fade-in, given the selection is at the end of the clip
questions.say_example: That applied a fade-in at the end of the clip. A fade-out is what's needed there.

questions.question: Does the level ramp between these two clips, or jump?
questions.why: Holding shift and dragging the clip's edge down creates a fade that prevents an abrupt, jarring drop to the -26.4 dB level.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to manually adjust the slope of the fade by ear to ensure the volume transition sounds perfectly natural.
questions.verify_form: The agent turned a level step into a fade - check the slope. Without the fade the drop is heard as a click.
questions.check: does the level change between these two clips ramp gradually rather than jump instantly to the new dB level
questions.say_example: The level drops straight to <-26.4> dB there. It's a step, with no ramp into it.

questions.question: Do you apply a fade-out to the end of the music clip?
